Reevaluating the decay mode $\tau \to \tau \gamma$, where $\tau$ refers to the tau lepton and $\gamma$ to the photon, is crucial for determining the electric dipole form factor with a precision of one percent. This study examines final states involving one photon and zero or one charged particle in $\tau$-pair production at the ILC, considering that both tau leptons decay semihadronically. The results show that, even when accounting for particle decays, the form factor uncertainty can be maintained at a level of one percent. In the case of zero-charged-particle decays, the form factor can be precisely determined due to the absence of significant backgrounds. However, in the case of one-charged-particle decays, the form factor can still be determined with high precision even when including semihadronic decays, thanks to the ILC's high energy and momentum resolution.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half.

Building upon a previous study that derived an integral expression for the product of two conformal field theory (CFT) operators, we extend this result to include spinning primaries in this work. Specifically, we have obtained a comprehensive expression for the product of two operators, one a spinning primary and the other a general secondary operator, which can be expressed in terms of conformal block operators satisfying the operator product expansion (OPE). Notably, we are able to provide an explicit integral representation for the OPE block operators primary operators, which significantly facilitates the computation of correlation functions in conformal field theories. As a consequence, we are able to derive a comprehensive set of equations that characterizes the OPE block operators, which essentially amounts to solving a generalized version of the Fuchsian differential equation. We anticipate that our findings will be instrumental in the analysis of OPE block spectra in conformal field theories.

Future experiments to study the cosmic microwave background will be able to measure a crucial parameter, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, with high precision. A key source of uncertainty in this measurement arises from lensing effects, which distort the patterns of microwave radiation. Delensing algorithms aim to mitigate this effect to improve the measurement's accuracy. Although research has shown that delensing can be effective at reducing the lensing impact, the impact of delensing itself introduces a new uncertainty that could potentially outweigh its benefits. In order to assess the efficacy of delensing, it is essential to understand the relationship between delensing and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. This study utilizes a variety of experiments and lensing delensing techniques to investigate this relationship and finds that delensing is generally capable of reducing the ratio's uncertainty by a factor of two for most experiments. However, the impact of delensing itself introduces a new uncertainty that could potentially outweigh its benefits. In order to assess the efficacy of delensing, it is essential to understand the relationship between delensing and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. This study utilizes a variety of experiments and lensing delensing techniques to investigate this relationship and finds that delensing is generally capable of reducing the ratio's uncertainty by a factor of two for most experiments.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths, allowing its analysis from pre-explosion to three years post-explosion. SN~2020jfo is classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short, brief photometric phase. Its spectra during the early stages show narrow Balmer lines and a prominent H-alpha absorption, alongside a distinctive [N II] doublet. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo's light curves exhibit a distinct interaction phase and a notable break around 100 days. Its explosion energy and interaction mass with the surrounding environment were determined, and its explosion site was analyzed to identify similarities with other supernovae. SN~2020jfo's progenitor was estimated to have a mass range of 12-18 solar masses, and its pre-explosion evolution lasted approximately 13 days. SN~2020jfo's long-term light curve and spectral data reveal a low-luminosity, narrow-line Type II supernova with minimal interaction and dust production.

To significantly enhance the collection capacity of wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye optics, it's proposed to utilize these optics in a multiplexing configuration. This approach involves splitting an X-ray detector's surface into multiple segments, each corresponding to a particular viewing direction, and assigning a specific lobster-eye optic to each segment. By doing so, the total number of segments can be substantial, far exceeding the number of optics available, which would otherwise limit its effectiveness. We investigate the benefits of this design by comparing its performance with and without multiplexing, taking into account factors including the number of optics, their arrangement, and the fraction of solid angle covered. It's found that a reasonable number of optics (around 10 to 20 per segment) is sufficient to achieve optimal results in this design. Furthermore, using 12 optics per segment in our model of the Wide Field X-ray Monitor (WFM) results in a factor of ~5 improvement in the detector's count rate, which is critical for accommodating the high flux expected from the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST).

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate how velocity information influences halo mass predictions, we ran dark matter simulations using the Einstein Telescope and Euclid configurations. We ran 32 different combinations of velocity and density initial conditions, including cases with velocity information and its absence, for a range of varying initial power spectrum conditions. We found that velocity information has little impact on halo mass predictions when density and velocity initial conditions follow the standard relation, but it has a significant effect (around 10%) when the ratio of power spectra between velocity and density becomes significantly different (by more than a factor of two). Furthermore, when the ratio of power spectra between velocity and density becomes more extreme (by more than a factor of ten), velocity information becomes crucial (around 30%) for accurately predicting halo mass.

Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, and the effectiveness of a proposed method is worth validating through objective evaluation metrics. Although various assessment techniques exist, they have limitations, such as reliance on pre-existing scores or time-consuming manual processing. In contrast, our research introduces a new approach that uses machine learning to automatically assess the accuracy of music transcription from audio, without requiring reference scores. By running the algorithm on multiple datasets, we found it capable of producing reliable results in a relatively short processing time, and we believe this method can be useful for both academic research and industry applications involving music processing.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, employs a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving geodesic equations. Our algorithm represents a significant improvement over previous methods, such as the post-Newtonian approximation, in accuracy. By utilizing this Lagrangian approach, we can directly account for effects like frame-dragging and the connection term, which would otherwise require artificial adjustments in post-Newtonian approximations. Our method includes a revised version of the Shapiro delay formula derived from first principles, which makes it an ideal tool for modeling stars in extreme mass-ratio binary systems involving compact objects.

A major hurdle in creating AI models that can automatically process complex documents like invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train them. One potential solution could be to train models on synthetic documents, but they would still need to be paired with real invoices to learn from. A novel approach allows a model to generate new documents on its own, without relying on paired data, by using a technique called unpaired image-to-document translation. They take this approach a step further by using a model that can generate documents at multiple scales, starting from low-resolution images and gradually adding more detail, and test it on the task of processing invoices and medical images. The results show that this approach can be effective, but it also has limitations, and future research could improve it by paying more attention to the details of the generated documents.

The collaboration between astronomers and gravitational wave researchers has led to a comprehensive classification of compact binary system mergers detected by LIGO and VIRGO. Through the analysis of event properties, they identified three distinct categories: Collapsar events, producing long-duration Gamma-Ray Bursts, binary neutron star mergers resulting in short GRBs, and neutron black hole mergers yielding no observable GRB.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been recognized. Although the concept of social determinants of health is not new, the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the significance of considering these factors in the context of healthcare access, utilization, and COVID-19-related risks. This study's primary objective is to provide an overview of the social determinants of health, their impact on healthcare, and relevant data sources that can be utilized in research and potential interventions.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios.

Urban settings are characterized by diverse physical encounters and social interactions that have a profound impact on economic productivity and innovation. To study these effects, researchers examine the behavior of professionals working in co-working spaces, who encounter diverse groups of people with various skills, leading to new collaboration opportunities. Examining member lists from 200 co-working spaces, spanning over 1.5 million member interactions, researchers develop a framework to analyze interactions and collaborate with an agent-based model. Empirical data on meeting frequencies and member attributes is used to simulate and test the model's predictions. Results show that diversity promotes innovation, however, the benefits of diversity depend on the distribution of skills. Furthermore, the optimal level of diversity is influenced by the distribution of skills among members.

The study of accretion bursts in young stellar objects is crucial to understanding the behavior of gravity-driven events. However, the duration of these events is often short, making it difficult to gather necessary data. A numerical approach has been taken to simulate accretion bursts in high-mass young stellar objects by considering various factors such as object orientation, disk structure, and other variables. The simulations reveal that the characteristics of accretion bursts are significantly influenced by the properties of the central object and its surrounding disk. The results show that the duration of these events can range from minutes to hours, which is consistent with observed burst durations. The study also finds that the spectral energy distributions and the light curves of the simulations exhibit the distinctive humps associated with accretion bursts. The simulations further suggest that the orientation of the disk with respect to the line of sight can greatly impact the characteristics of the bursts, particularly their duration and spectral energy distributions. The simulations will be used in conjunction with data from future radio surveys, such as the AREUS and the SURGY surveys, to identify accretion bursts and determine the properties of the high-mass young stellar objects within these regions.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in Buchholz's framework, we've derived multiple new theories, particularly those related to parafermion and superparafermion algebras.

Recent studies have assessed 5G base station exposure levels for children, teenagers, and adults, comparing them to safety guidelines. Evaluations utilized numerical models and real-world measurements to determine exposure, with results showing that all groups fall below recommended limits. Children and teenagers' exposure levels are similar to the general population, whereas adults' exposure is slightly lower. When considering the entire population, both calculated and measured evaluations confirm that exposure standards are met.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We consider a narrow-banded, monochromatic wave profile and modify the weak nonlinear theory to account for shear effects, resulting in a modified version of the Modulational Instability (MI) equation. Our study reveals that shear flow has a significant impact on the stability of waves, with both increased amplitude and phase shifts affected in a way that depends on the direction and strength of the flow. Notably, when the flow is oriented perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation, it induces a non-trivial phase shift that reverses sign as the flow's strength increases from negative to positive values, with a similar, though less pronounced, response observed for in-plane flow. Conversely, out-of-plane flow causes an unstable growth in amplitude, whereas in-plane flow results in stable amplitude behavior. These findings provide a foundation for understanding the effects of shear flow on water waves and suggest that further analysis of the MI equation is warranted to fully capture these dynamics.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through a differential form. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments poses a challenge for mobile robots. In conditions like heavy rain, snow, or fog, conventional sensors like GPS, lidar, radar, and cameras often malfunction. Mobile robots need alternative navigation approaches that can perform well in such scenarios. By leveraging their ability to maintain a consistent velocity, we propose using Doppler lidar to navigate through dynamic and changing environments. We utilize a Kalman filter estimator to estimate the robot's position, velocity, and attitude from Doppler lidar measurements of surrounding airflow. By running simulations in wind tunnels and outdoors, we evaluated the performance of this navigation approach. Results show that the method can accurately estimate its position, velocity, and attitude when subjected to various external influences, including airflow caused by moving obstacles and broader environmental conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of this approach to detect and respond to changes in airflow, indicating its potential to detect obstacles through the detection of changes in airflow.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose a novel deep learning approach, integrating character-level embeddings to enhance false news detection accuracy. In contrast to existing approaches that focus solely on semantic-level embeddings, our model leverages both semantic and graph-based character embeddings to represent news content. Experimental results indicate that our proposed character-based deep learning approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques while offering a computationally efficient solution for false news identification.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant change in a system's geometry is triggered by minor alterations in its underlying dynamics. The research also identified an important property of systems exhibiting this phenomenon – their instability. Furthermore, theoretical frameworks were developed to simulate the geometry of systems exhibiting the curvature effect, and these models were validated through numerical analysis and real-world applications.

In nonorthogonal multiple access systems, generating multiple access formats for multiple users over a single radio resource network involves a complex decoding problem. Due to the increased use of high-speed mobile and IoT devices, there's a growing need for faster decoding methods. Researchers have explored the concept of near-optimal decoding methods using different decoding order strategies. One such approach, known as the generalized d2O approach, has shown promising results but has a significant drawback of requiring prior knowledge of the system's signal-to-noise ratio. To address this limitation, a new decoding order strategy called d2O* is proposed, which achieves similar near-optimal performance without relying on prior SNR information. The d2O* approach is computationally efficient and has a linear complexity, making it suitable for real-world applications. Simulation results show that the proposed method performs within 0.5 dB of the optimal approach and has a linear complexity.

L1-PCA uses the L1 norm to calculate the position of the variance axis, which provides outlier-resistant results compared to conventional PCA. The L1 norm causes multiple PCs to emerge, which can be interpreted as distinct axes. To address this, a sorting step is applied to identify the most significant PC for each data point. Despite its effectiveness in reducing the impact of outliers, L1-PCA has limitations due to its computationally expensive calculations and the difficulty of interpreting the results. In contrast, our method uses a combination of outlier detection and removal to minimize the impact of outliers on the results while using only half the number of calculations required by L1-PCA.

Traditionally, social sciences researchers rely on qualitative and quantitative methods to study human behavior in groups. Recently, computational models can analyze online interactions on social media platforms. For example, the BERT model's performance improved significantly when trained on dialog annotations. However, annotating dialogs is a time-consuming and costly process. To streamline the process, researchers developed methods to leverage the models' annotations for training, but these methods require access to the dialogs' actual content. In contrast, our approach proposes the use of a pre-trained BERT model to guide human annotators and facilitate the process while maintaining the integrity of the annotations. In an experiment, a trained BERT model was used to generate a list of labels that human annotators could refer to, resulting in a 75% reduction in time spent annotating dialogs without a notable decrease in agreement among the annotators.

Kopczyński and Pitera initially posited that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to the equilibrium concept known as equilibria respecting energy conditions. We aim to expand upon this theory by examining specific cases of prefix-independent conditions and verifying that they indeed result in energy conditions. Furthermore, we acknowledge that these conditions are indeed equivalent to those proposed by Kopczyński and Pitera.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, suggesting that their soft interaction might produce high-energy phenomena. To explore this, researchers analyzed data from the INTEGRAL, Swift, and XMM-Newton space telescopes, focusing on a sample of four asynchronous polars that showed no hard X-ray emission when observed directly. By analyzing their soft X-ray spectra, researchers found evidence of high-temperature plasma, likely resulting from the accretion column's interaction with the binary's surroundings, and estimated its spin parameters with a certain degree of uncertainty, further supporting the hypothesis that soft X-ray emission in asynchronous polars is indeed caused by this interaction.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response, a novel map representation called the 'Hierarchical Topological Map' was designed to address these issues by combining local detailed maps with broader global structures. Although the system's ability to handle large-scale mapping was theoretically viable, its capabilities in practice were unclear. To test the HTM's feasibility, we developed a series of large-scale map construction tests using 3D laser scanners and a variety of real-world evaluations. The results showed that the system's state estimation component would consistently perform well in controlled conditions but would drift significantly in real-world scenarios. However, the HTM was found to effectively integrate local maps into a global structure even when the underlying slam algorithm drifted, demonstrating its potential for large-scale mapping.

The UM-IU@TUT system that took part in the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task 6 used BERT to create multiple sentence and character-based classifiers, which were then combined to identify offensive language in Twitter posts.  Although the team did not succeed in detecting abusive content as required by Subtask A, their models performed well in identifying the intensity of such content in Subtask C.  The UM-IU@TUT system, which used a single-layer LSTM to predict intensity, achieved a macro F1 score of 0.4336, ranking 7th out of 21 participants.  In addition, an analysis of the features extracted from the BERT model showed that the majority of attention weights were directed at negative intensities, which may indicate a problem with data imbalance.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within atomic interferometry, enabling a measurement of this effect. Based on simulations, it's possible to measure a field of 10 fg/cm^2 accuracy using atoms in the ground state of the 2S hyperfine level with a 10 cm interaction distance. Furthermore, this technique outperforms existing sensitivity measures for magnetic field detection.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model and considering both interlayer tunneling and Coulomb interactions, we find that strong interactions result in a half-metallic state with significant MCE, exceeding 1 K/watt in intensity. The magnitude of this effect can be adjusted through the distance between layers and the strength of the Coulomb interactions. Notably, the most notable MCE occurs at the interface, where the spin-polarized electron distribution allows for a large change in entropy with applied magnetic field. Our study highlights the MoTe$_2$-EuO heterostructure as an ideal system for magnetocaloric applications, leveraging the unique properties of two-dimensional materials to enhance the magnetocaloric effect.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior impact light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. Our analysis reveals that a quantum hydrodynamics model accurately captures the effects of spillover and nonlocality, even in situations where a local response model fails due to divergent fields. Notably, we find that the hydrodynamics model exhibits similar junction modes to the local response model, except with mode energies shifted by a factor of (1 - ε)^2, where ε represents the spillover factor.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs and constructs developed for the Calculus of Constructions, focusing on their relationships and the proof techniques employed, and concludes by discussing their implications for future research in this area.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of an on-site interaction. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum physics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure of density components, even when the number of identifiable components differs from the model's specified count. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately estimate the number of components, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.

We've derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude framework based on a color-ordered approach, and verified that the amplitude exhibits consistency with the duality to N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory at two loops. The method employs a novel type of integral called zigzag integral, which arises naturally in AdS space and is distinct from the standard class of non-trivial integrals found in flat space. The derivation of the two-loop amplitude also provides a clear illustration of the preamplitude's recursive nature as seen in flat space, and allows us to make a specific prediction for the coefficient of the $d^{4}\omega$ term in the three-loop anomalous magnetic moment of a bottom quark.

High-performance computing applications like Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) pose difficulties for conventional parallelism techniques due to shared memory access patterns causing performance bottlenecks. Actor-based parallelism offers a solution by minimizing data synchronization through independent task execution. Our research introduces a novel actor library, Parrot, which utilizes C++11's move semantics for efficient memory management. By leveraging C++11's type system and range-based algorithms, Parrot provides a high-level API for transparent memory optimization. Library benchmarks demonstrate that Parrot outperforms competing actor libraries while achieving near-native performance. Notably, our evaluation shows that Parrot can match the performance of OpenMP for SMMO workloads.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including the maximal operator, the potential operator, and several Calderón-Zygmund operators on the Lebesgue spaces $p\in (0,\infty)$. Specifically, we examine their boundedness on weighted spaces $L^p_p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and find conditions on the weights $p\in (0,\infty)$ that ensure the continuity of these operators. Moreover, we establish the equivalence of operator norms under these conditions, thus extending previous results obtained for specific operators or particular ranges of $p$.

By placing a non-magnetic impurity near a superconducting surface, researchers can manipulate the superconducting gap structure, potentially isolating the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. We utilize a model of an anisotropic s-wave superconducting gap to analyze this scenario. When the superconducting surface is rotated by a certain angle, the YSR states can become degenerate and exhibit distinct behaviors based on this angle, such as the formation of a nodal state, a constant state, or a vortex state. The rotation can also be used to map the superconducting gap structure and obtain the anisotropic gap parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an external magnetic field can be employed to control the YSR states by lifting their degeneracy and shifting their energies.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented in batch normalization space, resulting in a mask prediction. By bypassing feature extraction layers, FourierMask achieves higher accuracy and efficient instance segmentation compared to detection transformers. Specifically, our experiments show that FourierMask outperforms Mask R-CNN while having a 60% reduction in parameters and a 20% decrease in floating point operations on the MS COCO dataset.

This study investigates how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imagery fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers an alternative approach to cloud characterization, using a dataset of cloud optical thickness and location fromore. Although this method is theoretically viable, creating a tomographic reconstruction using passive satellite imagery is impractical due to the large differences in spatial resolution and data volume. Instead, using a semiempirical model of convective cloud formation, we developed a parametric approach that models the three-dimensional cloud morphology with a limited number of variables. We tested this approach using a dataset of cloud tomographic reconstructions from passive satellite imagery, first analyzing the relationship between the variables that define the cloud morphology and determine its entropy for various cloud types. The results show that cloud morphology entropy is higher for clouds thicker than 20 optical units and below 2 km altitude. It also varies less with wavelength and is generally higher for clouds with a larger vertical extent.

The impact of a laser pulse's chirp on the interaction with a relativistically self-modulated laser pulse and a thin layer of plasma is examined. It is discovered that a negatively chirped laser pulse requires a significantly lower plasma density to maintain pulse transmission, as this density is significantly lower than that required for unchirped or positively chirped pulses. As a result of this decreased plasma density, the formation of a thin, relativistically self-modulated plasma layer with comparable thickness to that produced by an intense, unchirped laser pulse becomes possible. Numerical simulations indicate that a thin, relativistically self-modulated plasma layer can result in the generation of a stable, monolithic electron spike with high charge density.

The early lives of young planets are significantly influenced by the gradual cooling of their surrounding disks, ultimately shaping the fate of these celestial bodies. A team of researchers has developed a comprehensive model to analyze the complex interplay between young planets, their disks, and the surrounding environment. Utilizing this model, scientists simulated numerous scenarios to study the diverse range of planetary systems, covering the evolution of planets from their formation to their eventual stability or instability. According to their findings, the destiny of young planets is largely determined by the interplay of three key factors: the gradual cooling of their disks, the influx of external objects, and the initial conditions of their formation. By analyzing these processes, researchers were able to identify distinct periods in the evolution of young planets. In the first phase, lasting around 100 million years, the behavior of planets is largely shaped by their disks. As their disks evolve, planets enter a second phase, influenced by the influx of external objects, and finally, in the third phase, lasting around 10 billion years, their evolution is largely determined by their initial conditions.

We examined the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To achieve this, we used a computational approach that accounts for electron correlations.  Our findings indicate that when these defects occupy substitutional sites, they behave as half-filled bands with similar spinless characteristics.  However, when positioned on oxygen sites, they exhibit different characteristics, with nitrogen forming a $\pi$ bond with surrounding oxygen atoms and displaying a spin of 1.5, and carbon displaying a spin of 1 when present in a $\pi$-bonding state.  Our study suggests that nitrogen on oxygen sites could be an efficient method for creating stable, free-spin electron reserves within TiO2.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through measuring the momentum of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of using this new variable to distinguish signal events featuring top-quark pairs from background events featuring $t\bar{t}W\gamma, t\bar{t}Z, t\bar{t}b\bar{b}, t\bar{t}jj$, and $b\bar{b}jj$ in the ATLAS detector's kinematic reconstruction. By applying a cut to the new variable, the background can be significantly reduced to less than 0.1 of the signal for an integrated luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays have provided valuable insights into its dynamics, revealing that its state is not in thermodynamic equilibrium as initially assumed. To accurately determine the dynamics of the intra-cluster medium, it is essential to correctly account for its non-thermal pressure support. Non-thermal pressure support plays a crucial role in cluster mergers, influencing the dynamics of the intra-cluster medium and affecting gas accretion and star formation within the cluster. In the context of the MW, the dynamics of the intra-cluster medium are complex, with its structure shaped by the interaction with the Milky Way. The presence of the MW's tidal tail and its impact on the intra-cluster medium's dynamics are areas that require further research. The study of the intra-cluster medium's dynamics is critical to our understanding of the MW's place within the LM. The LM's dynamics are influenced by a network of filaments and clusters, with a significant portion of its mass-energy budget attributed to magnetic fields and cosmic rays. The study of the intra-cluster medium's dynamics in the LM can provide valuable insights into the evolution of the LM and the MW's role within it. The detection of a possible shock wave in the LM, as well as the discovery of the MW's interaction with the LM's gas, have significantly expanded our understanding of the MW's intra-cluster medium. The study of the MW's intra-cluster medium has also led to a better understanding of the MW's chemical evolution and its relation to the LM's

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically considering the minimum density of a subsequence that exhibits the same pattern of ordering as the original sequence. Building upon their work, they provided a limit inferior of approximately 0.5 for sequences of natural numbers in ascending order. However, they were unable to determine if this limit inferior could be as low as 1/2. Now, in our research, we have found that indeed this limit inferior can be as low as 1/2.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like structure composed of various molecular regions. Within the CMZ, a notable area is the Large Megallanic Cloud-like structure (LMC-like), which exhibits an unusual three-dimensional gas density pattern. Researchers employed sensitive radio telescope observations, utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), to study the gas and star formation within LMC-like by analyzing multiple molecular lines. Their findings show that LMC-like is an isolated feature in the CMZ, with a unique axis running perpendicular to the local standard of rest. The data also reveal that the gas within LMC-like lacks the typical spiral arm density enhancements commonly found in other molecular clouds in the CMZ. As a result, the cloud remains under-dense along the plane of the sky and over-dense in the perpendicular direction. The ALMA observations of LMC-like revealed an overall ring-like shape, with a diameter of approximately 60 parsecs, and the detection of various molecular lines indicating active star formation, coupled with the presence of massive young stellar clusters, further supports this cloud's distinct nature.

This study proposes a novel eye disorder classification method that utilizes eye movements and blinking patterns to detect Bell's Palsy. Since current methods primarily focus on static eye images, our approach incorporates the analysis of eye motion and blinking frequency to differentiate between healthy individuals, Bell's Palsy patients, and patients with facial paralysis caused by stroke. Our system consists of multiple components, including eye motion and blinking pattern extraction, feature learning using a convolutional neural network, and decision-making through support vector machine. We tested this system using 20 subjects, including 10 healthy individuals and 10 subjects with eye disorders, and achieved a high accuracy rate of 85%.

Our investigation highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator, our findings show that even with approximate gates, qudits exhibit greater resistance to decoherence compared to qubits, largely due to the increased dimensionality allowing for more effective error cancellation. Notably, with catalytic purifiable noise, qudits outperform qubits, demonstrating a significant advantage of using multi-level systems in quantum computations.

When an intense laser interacts with a solid material, it produces a high-energy pulse of positrons through the process of laser-induced pair production. However, due to the short length of the positron pulse compared to the original pulse of light, the polarization state becomes less defined. Our research utilizes a quantum electrodynamics model to analyze the polarization state of the generated positrons and demonstrates that it is heavily influenced by the number of photons in the laser pulse, the thickness of the solid target, and the LIPPD process itself. Notably, we find that the polarization degree of the positrons can be controlled by adjusting the characteristics of the laser pulse and the target, thereby enabling the potential for producing highly polarized positron beams.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that is linear (i.e., proportional to the number of elements) for a specific, large subset of generators. In particular, it is proven that linear diameter does not necessarily imply a small abelian subgroup, and some new classes of groups are identified where linear diameter is guaranteed, such as groups with a high proportion of involutions or nilpotent groups with a specific, small class of generators.

This research introduces a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor that utilizes a diverse set of thermal voltages to accurately determine temperature across a wide range of -20 to 120 degrees Celsius. The temperature sensor's design leverages dynamic voltage and frequency scaling to minimize power consumption while maintaining system performance. A 65-nanometer CMOS process was utilized to fabricate the temperature sensor, and it was incorporated into a test chip alongside DVS/DFS circuits. The experimental results show that the temperature sensor precisely estimates temperature with an error of 2.5 degrees Celsius and distinguishes between warm areas of the chip and cooler areas with a resolution of 0.1 degrees Celsius. Furthermore, the temperature sensor's ability to detect thermal gradients was validated at various temperatures and supply voltages.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap stars, as well as the origins of the strong magnetic fields found in white dwarfs and neutron stars, remain topics of interest. Historically, studies have focused on stable magnetic configurations such as dipolar and quadrupolar structures. However, research has revealed that certain twisted magnetic configurations, previously considered unstable, can in fact persist for extended periods when stellar convection zones impede heat flux disparities. Using this knowledge, researchers have derived new limits on the maximum allowed strength of twisted magnetic fields in white dwarfs and neutron stars, finding them to be significantly more stable than their dipolar counterparts. Furthermore, studies suggest that twisted magnetic fields may be more prevalent in the population of magnetic white dwarfs.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven effective in studying complex systems through the renormalization group flow equation. By continuously adjusting a cutoff to confine the system to successively narrower ranges, the FRG method determines how the system's parameters evolve. In response, researchers have developed various flow equations, each tailored to a specific context, drawing on the underlying principles of this equation. In an effort to standardize the approach, this study proposes a formal framework for deriving flow equations based on the FRG technique's underlying assumptions. By examining the underlying assumptions of the FRG method, researchers can derive flow equations that reflect the system's behavior under changes in the cutoff. In addition, the study demonstrates how the established framework can be applied to other systems by transforming the flow equations into an alternative, more manageable form. As a result, the study provides a unified perspective on the FRG technique and its applications.

Music enthusiasts still heavily rely on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

Taking a Lie groupoid as input, researchers have an interest in understanding a specific map called the Chern-Weil map. This map connects the Lie algebraic concept of differential forms to the geometric concept of connections on a specific type of bundle called a principal bundle. The main focus of this study is on examining the higher gauge theory related to the Chern-Weil map, and it has established connections with various concepts such as gerbes and algebroids. The research has also been generalized to apply to more complex structures like Lie groupoids and stack-based structures like Lie algebroids.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to have a greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass differences significant at the p=0.02 level.  Notably, the mass disparity between these core types is not observed at 8 um, indicating that the difference is confined to higher mass ranges and suggesting the presence of a mass threshold.  This threshold is estimated to be around 10-20 solar masses, above which cores are likely to contain a protostar, while cores with masses below this threshold may remain starless for an extended period.  Such a threshold is consistent with the idea that a minimum mass is required to collapse a core, but may also indicate the influence of other factors, such as magnetic fields, in limiting the mass-to-ratio of protostellar cores.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators that preserve finiteness, alongside their corresponding classes of forest frames for Godel modal logics. The study specifically examines the relational semantics for the subvarieties of finite Godel algebra-based modal logics that extend intutionistic and classical modal logic, including the novel logics of Forest Godel and its classical counterpart.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable insights for environmental monitoring, urban planning, and development, among other areas. Yet, their full potential remains untapped due to the complexity of the data. This complexity stems from the sheer volume of points, which often surpasses millions, and the variety of shapes and sizes present, making it difficult to create compact descriptors. Current methods either focus on specific features or employ deep learning techniques, which struggle to generalize across different scenarios and often disregard contextual information. This thesis proposes a novel approach, the Regional Contextual LiDAR Descriptor (ReCoLiD), which extracts context-aware descriptors from LiDAR point clouds. ReCoLiD first identifies local patterns and regions within the data before creating compact descriptors. This proposed approach outperforms existing methods, demonstrating enhanced classification and segmentation performance, and is versatile enough for use in a range of applications.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been a valuable tool for researchers. Building upon the framework of zonal functions introduced by Gelfand and Turaev, this concept has been expanded to the sphere, S^d. Researchers are particularly interested in determining the conditions that make a given expansion of a zonal function, in terms of Gegenbauer polynomials, indeed positive definite. This study takes a closer look at the recurrence relation between the coefficients of such an expansion and the space dimension, d, and subsequent dimensions, d+1 and d+2, as a means to better understand the positive definiteness of a zonal function on S^d.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper presents a novel method for linking neutrino and UHECR events from existing datasets. It employs a statistical approach to identify overdensities in UHECR maps that correlate with the arrival directions of neutrino events. Utilizing the most current datasets from IceCube and ANTARES for neutrinos and the Pierre Auger Observatory for UHECRs, this method reveals a notable excess in the UHECR dataset around the direction of the most energetic neutrino, with a probability of occurrence being p-value 0.02. Furthermore, the method identifies additional excesses at lower energies, specifically around the directions of two other highly energetic neutrino events reported previously.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at low shear rates. Research has revealed three distinct friction modes - slippage, roughness filling, and jamming - that arise from interactions between the surface microstructure and viscoelastic properties of the liquid. Although these interactions have an impact on the composition of lubricants, suspensions, and emulsions, among other liquids, the specific conditions required to enter each regime are not well-defined. This study investigates the relationship between the composition of binary mixtures of surfactant and polymer solutions and their roughness-induced friction behavior, and demonstrates how adjusting the solution components can manipulate viscosity, slippage, and surface roughness to preferentially target one friction mode over the others.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier model comprising nine individual classifiers, each responsible for detecting a specific skin cancer type. To verify the validity of our approach, we tested an alternative model without the anomaly-aware modification on the entire dataset of nine classes, removing one class at a time to account for actual data composition. To distinguish cancerous images from healthy ones, we entered the anomaly-aware model into the challenge, and the results showed strong performance.

The behavior of an elastic membrane, confining two fluids of differing densities in a rotating system, is examined under the influence of gravity and an external pressure. When the membrane is subjected to small deformations, its appearance changes in a complex manner due to interactions between curvature-driven diffusion, rotation, gravity, and an external pressure, as well as the differing densities of the fluids. A combination of linear and nonlinear analyses is utilized to study the membrane's behavior, revealing the emergence of a fingering instability influenced by curvature-driven diffusion, rotation, gravity, and the elastic properties of the membrane. Notably, rotation is found to induce an elastic instability corresponding to a specific membrane mode, and this elastic instability can be induced by varying the rotation rate, even in the absence of gravity, a phenomenon not observed in non-elastically confined fluids.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as negative work, with no associated temperature change, confirming that it represents a thermodynamic force that drives the system towards equilibrium. Interestingly, we find that work is positive, indicating an increase in entropy due to the thermalization of the system.

Researchers have detected the formation of a specific intermediate, ethynyl benzene, through the collision of benzene molecules with high-speed ethynyl radicals at various temperatures, as reported in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition. Additionally, by comparing their findings to theoretical calculations, they were able to confirm its existence and determine its stability. An intermediate with the same properties was also discovered in 2018, but it was not as stable as ethynyl benzene and was formed through a different process. Ethynyl benzene is thought to be a crucial step in the formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in interstellar spaces, and its detection through radio telescopes remains elusive due to its predicted column density being too low. However, it is worth continuing to search for it in regions rich in molecules, such as the Eagle Nebula, in the future.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, due to the lack of syntactic regularization. We introduce a novel attention model, the Conditional Random Field attention model, which incorporates context from all previously generated target words, while limiting its dependence to ensure translation quality. We evaluate our approach on standard NIST Chinese-English and WMT German-English translation tasks, and the results show significant improvements in BLEU scores, with a 1.32% increase for the Chinese-English task and a 0.53% increase for the German-English task.

The significant disparity between healthcare advancement and health outcomes can be addressed through translational medicine. This issue provides a comprehensive introduction to various aspects of translational medicine by employing systems thinking, analyzing the complex interconnections within the healthcare system, and highlighting potential risks of fragmented solutions. It also introduces a holistic approach to addressing challenges in clinical research, healthcare practice, education, and policy-making. By illustrating examples of successful translational initiatives, it demonstrates the potential of this approach to promote a culture of collaboration and facilitate meaningful solutions.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to reduce to established dark matter and dark energy cosmologies under specific conditions. Using a novel transformation, a previously intractable self-gravity problem in the unified framework has been resolved. A modified version of the Einstein-Boltzmann equations has been derived, enabling numerical simulations of the universe's evolution. These simulations demonstrate the existence of a stable, dark energy-dominated period of expansion, consistent with observations. The model's self-gravity solution reveals the emergence of a dark energy 'cosmological constant' and an equation of state parameter 'omega' that evolve over time. The evolution of 'omega' is found to be consistent with the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) model's predictions for a vacuum universe. The model also exhibits the phenomenon of gravitational dissolution, where dark matter is dispersed by dark energy's expansive force. The simulations show that the model's dark matter and dark energy densities follow a power-law relationship, with 'omega' evolving from negative to positive values. The model predicts that the universe's dark energy density will continue to dominate, with 'omega' approaching zero as the universe expands further.

In educational settings, curiosity is a vital skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a key to personal and societal development.  However, curiosity appears to be in decline, and this decline seems to be linked to the rising fear of making mistakes.  This fear is, in turn, fueled by the way students are evaluated, and the emphasis placed on grades over growth.  In order to reverse this trend, we need to redefine what success means in an educational system, and make sure that making mistakes is seen as an essential part of the learning process.  In this talk, I will present a theoretical framework that views curiosity as a type of metacognitive skill, and discuss the ways in which this skill can be developed through the use of games and challenges that encourage exploration and risk-taking.  I will also present data from a pilot study that shows that, with the right approach, students can be taught to be more curious, and that this curiosity can transfer to other areas of their lives.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs, ultimately demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes preserve the desirable properties of their Euclidean space counterparts. This modification allows our model to accommodate the unique characteristics of graph-structured data, including flexibility in choosing the graph Laplacian and its corresponding spectral properties. This flexibility is critical in the analysis of real-world graphs, which are often characterized by irregular shapes and varying neighborhood sizes. This is further illustrated through an example involving the approximation of a function defined on a tree graph, which shows that our method outperforms other common Gaussian process models in the Euclidean space, particularly in scenarios where the function is highly non-linear.

Current urban road network sensing methods suffer from high costs, limited coverage, and biased data collection. For rapid urban planning and efficient traffic management, accurate and comprehensive knowledge of the road network is essential. To bridge this gap, we propose listeningDevice, a pioneering approach that utilizes off-the-shelf audio equipment mounted on moving vehicles to gather sensory data about the road network. By analyzing audio recordings, we leverage machine learning models to extract valuable insights from the surroundings, such as detecting lane changes, identifying road conditions, and recognizing surrounding infrastructure. Through large-scale experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of listeningDevice in sensing urban road networks, revealing notable correlations between the acquired data and actual network measurements. Furthermore, we showcase the scalability of our approach by successfully applying it to diverse scenarios, including different cities, weather conditions, and audio sampling rates.

The ATOMKI group has been investigating the invisible decay of $J/	au$ mesons, which could indicate the existence of light sterile neutrinos. To better understand how invisible $J/	au$ decays work, we have reevaluated existing data from experiments that used two methods to measure these decays. Our analysis shows that we can learn more about invisible $J/	au$ decays if we know more about how these decays are affected by electron-anti-electron pairs, which can be created when $J/	au$ mesons interact with other particles. Knowing this interaction better will help us understand invisible $J/	au$ decays and potential light sterile neutrinos. To achieve this, we created an equation that takes into account the probability of $J/	au$ mesons turning into electron-anti-electron pairs as well as the probability of these pairs being detected. If we know this equation and the factors that influence it, we can use existing data on $J/	au$ mesons that turn into visible particles, such as electron pairs, to estimate the invisible decays. Using this approach with past experiments that measured the total $J/	au$ meson decay rate, we created a new way to estimate the invisible decay rate. This method allows us to estimate the invisible decay rate as a percentage of the total decay rate, which is around 10.4%, which is consistent with previous estimates. However,

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through applications to multiple types of multivariate time series signals, including functional multivariate time series, vector autoregressive processes, and stochastic processes defined by stochastic integrals.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making the delivery of testing programs possible again. The success of these systems relies on multiple factors including robust training data collection methods, model architecture, performance metrics, evaluation protocols, and data protection regulations. A scoring system's ability to accurately assess student learning and provide unbiased results heavily depends on its own integrity. A notable example is the case of the Graduate Record Examination (GRE) automated essay scoring system developed by ETS, in which the code was leaked on GitHub, allowing users to manipulate the scoring algorithm. The code comprises PyTorch models that utilize recurrent neural networks to analyze essay content and assign scores based on the learned features. The possibility of the code being used for malicious purposes raises concerns about the potential for manipulation of the code's output, thereby undermining the evaluation process. The issue is further complicated by the absence of protocols for evaluating the fairness, security, and robustness of such systems. The provided code also raises questions about data collection methods used for training the models, as it appears to contain sensitive information. The presence of this code in the public domain highlights the need for the development of more transparent and auditable automated assessment systems.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\beta}$ holds for the probability of a random walk being non-negative at time $x$ and for the probability of a L\'evy process being above a certain level at time $x$, where the parameter $\beta$ is determined by the second moment of the step distribution. If the step distribution has a power law tail with index $1 < \alpha \le 2$, then the decay rate $\beta$ is not determined by the tail index alone, but instead depends on the entire distribution, except when $\alpha = 2$ which results in $\beta = 1/2$. The condition $\alpha \ge 2$ is necessary for the decay to be non-integrable, but integrable power law decay occurs for $1 < \alpha < 2$.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability using a fast magnetic probe capable of measuring small changes in magnetic field strength. By analyzing the measurements and comparing them to theoretical models, it was determined that the plasma source does indeed operate in helicon mode.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

Accurate identification of cancer cells through segmentation relies on the precise detection of cell nuclei. Nucleus segmentation models, particularly point-attention U-Net, have shown high performance but are difficult to train due to their complex optimization process. To overcome this challenge, a new approach called CoPA-PU-Net has been developed, integrating coordinate point attention into the point-attention U-Net network. This innovative model simplifies the optimization process while maintaining high performance, as evidenced by its top-ranked submission to the CVC-12 dataset challenge, achieving a Dice coefficient of 0.9362. Furthermore, CoPA-PU-Net has demonstrated robust performance on the BCDR dataset, outperforming existing methods with a Dice coefficient of 0.9345, demonstrating its potential for use in real-world applications.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper builds upon prior work by Bernstein and Reznikov in order to establish the local converse theorem for the supercuspidal representations within the specified group types. 

Given two distinct, irreducible admissible generic representations of the group G, denoted as \pi_1(\sigma_1,\tau_1) and \pi_2(\sigma_2,\tau_2) respectively, with their underlying local fields being the same, we can determine if these two representations are equivalent. This equivalence holds true if and only if the underlying local fields F_1 and F_2 are the same, and if the underlying Weil groups \sigma_1 and \sigma_2 as well as the underlying Dirac twists \tau_1 and \tau_2 are also the same. 

This paper's main contribution also includes the establishment of a precise formula to compute the local gamma factors. Furthermore, this computation is performed without relying on the Archimedean field's properties, thus making this approach distinct from prior methods.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Pyroptosis, a form of cell death that results from inflammasome activation, plays a significant role in defending against pathogenic infections. The NLRP3 inflammasome is the most extensively studied and widely expressed inflammasome complex, responsible for initiating pyroptosis in response to various stimuli. However, the precise mechanism by which the NLRP3 inflammasome is activated across different cell types remains unclear. This review aims to provide an in-depth examination of the NLRP3 inflammasome activation process, pyroptosis, and associated regulatory pathways. Furthermore, we discuss the recent findings on the role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in pyroptosis across different cell types and its implications for our understanding of this complex biological process.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized to investigate its impact on the capacity of Markov decision processes to be learned through reinforcement learning. Theoretical evidence is provided to illustrate that learning these processes generally requires significantly more episodes of interaction with the environment than processes unaffected by external factors. A new algorithm is proposed, utilizing additional learning pathways to mitigate the disruptive effects of unanticipated state and reward fluctuations on the learning process. Through analysis and empirical testing, the benefits of this approach are demonstrated, particularly its ability to handle situations involving unanticipated reward signals.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is activated upon confirmation in a specific predetermined condition. However, the verification of these conditions before the contract's activation has significant implications for maintaining the integrity of the entire blockchain network. The activation of a malicious contract can lead to devastating consequences, such as stealing funds from users or creating unnecessary transactions, ultimately causing network congestion. The verification process we propose is designed to ensure that only contracts that meet specific criteria can be activated within a blockchain network. The method we use to achieve this is through the integration of blockchain technology with the theory of streaming algorithms, enabling the efficient verification of the conditions of a contract in real-time. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the development of concrete examples of blockchain networks and streaming algorithms, and the verification time complexity is analyzed and shown to be directly proportional to the size of the input data.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained significant attention in recent years. Convolution layers in GCNNs are used to extract pattern information from graph-organized data, enabling the extension of neural networks to non-Euclidean topologies. This paper presents an innovative approximation method for calculating convolutions in GCNNs, utilizing Random Fourier Features (RFFs). By leveraging the properties of random linearization, our approach circumvents the need for explicit eigendecomposition of graph matrices. This is particularly beneficial as the eigendecomposition process becomes computationally unfeasible for large-scale real-world applications. Our proposed method is efficient, easy to implement, and outperforms existing approximation techniques in terms of accuracy and computational performance. Moreover, the simplicity of our approach facilitates seamless integration with optimized backpropagation methods. The code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/ahmedosama/RFF-GCNN.

In a theory with scalar fields and a SU(2) gauge field, solutions that combine soliton and black hole characteristics have been identified. These solutions are only possible when the holonomy constraint, which ensures the holonomy of the connection is zero, is imposed on a spacetime configuration consisting of a soliton and an anti-soliton at infinity. Removing this constraint allows the solution to be reinterpreted as a black hole with non-compact internal space. A new solution has been found where the holonomy constraint is non-trivial, resulting in a spacetime that includes both a soliton and a black hole.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Elastography, an imaging technique used to assess tissue stiffness, is vulnerable to artifacts caused by boundary effects and limited sampling depth. The Synthetic Aperture (SA) technique improves upon earlier methods for reconstructing elastography images. However, the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method was found to outperform traditional SA methods in a previous study. This paper provides VSSA's underlying theory and a detailed description of its implementation, including a discussion of its computational efficiency. A comparison with the traditional SA technique is also made to illustrate the VSSA's enhanced performance in terms of point spread function and sampling depth. Ultimately, the benefits of the VSSA method make it a promising approach for elastography imaging.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach to logical pseudocodes provides a means of verifying complex systems by translating them into executable code based on natural deduction, which in turn allows for the application of advanced verification techniques originally developed for programs.

The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets obtained from chains with minimal elements combined into a V-shaped structure.
